title: What If Gravity Dropped by Half Tomorrow?

lines.text: Gravity just got cut in half.
It's seven in the morning, tomorrow, and your alarm is going off.
You reach for your phone and knock it off the nightstand.
And it falls slowly, like someone pressed slow motion.
It takes about 40 percent longer to hit the floor.
visual: Fall time grows as gravity drops

lines.text: You sit up, and your whole body lifts off the mattress for a second.
You laugh, because your bed suddenly feels like a trampoline.
Your phone is buzzing on the floor with the same message on every screen.
Overnight, Earth's pull on everything dropped to exactly half.
Nobody knows why, and nobody knows if it's coming back.
Every news channel has a physicist on, and every physicist looks nervous.
You weigh half, things fall slower, and the air just got thinner.
This is The Survivometer.
visual: HOUR BY HOUR. ONE FULL YEAR.

lines.text: We'll live through it hour by hour, and work out your odds of making it one full year.
Right now, it's a coin flip, fifty percent.
Eight in the morning, and your street has turned into a playground.
Kids are jumping over parked cars.
A teenager clears the hood of a minivan and lands laughing.
Your neighbor dunks a basketball for the first time in his life.
Then you hear the first crash.
A delivery van slides right through a red light with its brakes locked.
Nobody is hurt, but the driver stares at his tires like they betrayed him.
Tires grip the road by pressing down on it, and now they press half as hard.
So every car needs twice the distance to stop.
visual: Braking distance grows as grip drops

lines.text: Your car keys are sitting on the kitchen counter.
Drive to work like normal, or stay put?
You stay put and watch three more cars slide past your window.
Somewhere across town, a bus misses its stop by half a block.
Staying off the road moves your odds to fifty five.
One in the afternoon, and you have a pounding headache.
You climb one flight of stairs and have to stop and breathe.
Air pressure is just the weight of all the air above you.
visual: THE WEIGHT OF THE AIR ABOVE YOU

lines.text: Half the gravity means half the weight, so half the pressure.
Until today, you only found air that thin at 18,000 feet.
visual: Where air pressure is half (until today)

lines.text: That's higher than Everest Base Camp.
Trekkers take more than a week to walk up there, so their bodies can adjust.
You got there overnight.
So did every person on the planet, all at the same moment.
Your heart is pounding just from walking to the kitchen.
And you live in Denver, a mile above sea level.
Here, the air now feels like over 20,000 feet.
visual: What Denver's air feels like now
Estimate: half of Denver's normal pressure

lines.text: Outside, people are bouncing down the sidewalk and racing each other for fun.
One by one, they sit down on the curb, gasping.
Jump around like everyone else, or sit still and breathe?
Mountain doctors have one rule: go slow, drink water, and if it gets worse, go down.
visual: IF IT GETS WORSE, GO DOWN

lines.text: You lie on the couch, sip water, and take slow, deep breaths.
Sitting still pushes your odds to fifty eight.
Seven forty in the evening, and the map on your phone has frozen.
Your little blue dot is drifting across a field you've never been to.
Every satellite was flying at exactly the speed it needed to stay in orbit.
To escape Earth, a satellite needs about 41 percent more speed.
visual: EXTRA SPEED NEEDED TO ESCAPE ORBIT

lines.text: Cut Earth's pull in half, and that extra speed drops to zero.
So tonight, every satellite in orbit is quietly drifting off into space.
No GPS, no satellite TV, and no weather forecasts.
Your weather app is stuck on yesterday's forecast.
Then the TV flickers, and the lights go out.
Dams make electricity from falling water.
The water now falls with half the force, so every dam makes half the power.
visual: Dam power = water weight x drop height

lines.text: The power company starts rolling blackouts, one neighborhood at a time.
Your street goes dark for two hours, then the next street takes its turn.
Trust your phone's maps, or find a paper map?
You dig an old road atlas out of the garage.
The paper map lifts your odds to sixty.
Day three, and you still can't sleep through the night.
You wake up gasping every hour or two.
You try to cook pasta, and it's still hard after twenty minutes.
You switch to a pressure cooker, the trick every mountain town already knows.
With half the air pressure, water boils at only about 180 degrees.
The emergency rooms are full of people who can't catch their breath.
Hospitals are handing out oxygen, but there isn't enough for everyone.
You remember the doctors' rule: if it gets worse, go down.
The Gulf Coast sits a whole mile lower than Denver.
Stay in Denver, or drive down to the coast?
You pack water, food, and the road atlas.
Your neighbor with a weak heart asks for a ride, and you say yes.
You fill the tank while the pumps still have power.
Leaving the mountains lifts your odds to sixty two.
Week one, and you're on the road at dawn.
The highway is lined with cars that stopped too late.
Every curve and every exit now takes twice the room it used to.
70 on the highway, or 40 on the back roads?
You take the back roads, slow and steady.
A two day drive takes you six.
In every small town, the fountain in the square shoots twice as high.
At a rest stop, a dog clears a picnic table in one jump.
Your neighbor sleeps most of the way, wrapped in a blanket in the back seat.
At night, you look up, and something about the sky is wrong.
The Moon looks a little smaller than it did last night.
It was moving at its old orbital speed too, so it's leaving, just like the satellites.
On day six, you finally see the ocean.
You roll down the window and take the deepest breath you've had all week.
The air at sea level is still thin, but it's the best air left in the country.
Reaching the coast lifts your odds to sixty four.
Month one, and you're renting a room in a beach town in Texas.
Your headaches are fading.
Your body is building extra red blood cells, the same way mountain climbers adjust.
But now there's a quieter problem.
Bones stay strong by carrying weight, and yours now carry half.
Astronauts in space lose about 1 to 1.5 percent of their bone each month.
visual: BONE LOST PER MONTH BY ASTRONAUTS

lines.text: Half gravity is not zero gravity, and nobody knows exactly how fast bones weaken here.
visual: HOW FAST BONES WEAKEN AT HALF GRAVITY

lines.text: Lie on the couch, or train every day?
You fill a backpack with sand and walk the beach every morning.
Heavy backpacks, stairs, and jumping are your new medicine.
Your neighbor joins you, slow at first, then every single morning.
Meanwhile, the whole world is learning new tricks.
One mover carries a whole couch up the stairs alone.
High school basketball raises its hoops by three feet.
At a local track meet, a sixteen year old breaks the long jump world record.
Training every day pushes your odds to sixty seven.
Year one, and the Moon is gone from the night sky.
All that's left is a bright point of light, drifting in its own orbit around the Sun.
With no satellites, the world went back to radio, paper maps, and landlines.
And here is the twist.
Humans already live in air almost this thin.
La Rinconada, a gold mining town in Peru, sits at about 16,700 feet.
visual: La Rinconada, Peru. Highest town on Earth

lines.text: Tens of thousands of people live and work there every day.
Their bodies adapted, and slowly, so does everyone else's.
Engineers rebuild brakes, and cars come back to the roads, slower and safer.
Airlines fly again, after engineers redo every calculation.
Kids born this year will never know what heavy feels like.
So, what were your odds?
If you drove to work, jumped around, and stayed in Denver, the Survivometer gives you six percent.
If you stayed put, rested, went down to the coast, and trained every day, your odds are seventy one percent.
The difference was never strength.
It was going slow while everyone else was jumping.
Tell us in the comments: what's the first thing you would do with half gravity?
And tell us which scenario the Survivometer should run next.
See you in the next what if.
